name: french onion vegetable soup
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS. Variant A is the classical french onion soup shape — deeply caramelized onions in beef stock, gruyere gratin, white beans folded in for protein (personalization). Variant B extends into a broader vegetable soup — same caramelized onion + white wine + gruyere gratin framework, but with a wider mix of vegetables (celery root, turnips, carrots, garlic, ginger root) and a ginger + turmeric herb axis instead of thyme. NO potatoes in either variant (see variant B notes).

=== VARIANT A — CLASSICAL FRENCH ONION SOUP (WITH WHITE BEANS FOR PROTEIN) ===

Classical french onion soup — deeply caramelized onions in beef stock, topped with toasted bread and broiled gruyere. White beans folded in for protein (see notes).

INGREDIENTS:
- 4-5 large yellow onions, thinly sliced
- 4 tbsp butter
- 2 tbsp olive oil (to cut the butter for smoke point)
- 1 bay leaf
- fresh thyme (a few sprigs)
- 1/2 to 3/4 cup dry white wine (deglaze)
- 6-8 cups beef stock (vegetable stock also works — see notes)
- 1 can white beans (cannellini or great northern), drained and rinsed
- 1 baguette or similar bread, sliced into rounds and toasted
- shredded gruyere cheese (generous — enough to blanket each bowl)
- pinch of turmeric (secret ingredient — see notes)
- fresh parsley (finish)
- salt and black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. DEEPLY CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: melt butter with olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions and a small pinch of salt. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 45-60 minutes until the onions are deeply browned — a rich mahogany color, not just golden. This is the load-bearing technique (see notes). Don't rush with high heat; you want the caramelization to develop, not the onions to burn.
2. DEGLAZE WITH WINE: pour in the white wine and scrape up any browned fond from the bottom of the pot. Let it reduce briefly.
3. ADD STOCK + HERBS: pour in the beef stock. Add the bay leaf, thyme, and a pinch of turmeric. Bring to a simmer.
4. FOLD IN WHITE BEANS: add the drained white beans to the simmering broth. Simmer for 15-20 min to integrate.
5. TASTE AND ADJUST: salt and pepper to taste. Fish out the bay leaf and thyme stems (leaves can stay).
6. TOAST THE BREAD: while the soup simmers, slice the baguette into rounds and toast until crisp and lightly browned.
7. GRATIN + SERVE: ladle the hot soup into oven-safe bowls (ideally). Top each bowl with a toasted bread round or two, then a generous mound of shredded gruyere. Broil under the oven's broiler until the cheese is deeply melted and browned in spots (2-4 min — watch closely; broilers vary).
8. Scatter fresh parsley on top. Serve immediately, hot.

=== VARIANT B — BROADER VEGETABLE SOUP (GINGER + CELERY ROOT + POTATOES + CARROTS) ===

Extends the classical french onion framework into a broader vegetable soup. Same caramelized onion base, same white wine deglaze, same gruyere gratin finish — but with a wider set of vegetables and a different herb axis (ginger + turmeric instead of thyme). NO TOMATO. This is where the pure-vegetable idea originally drafted in french-beef-and-mushroom-stew landed after being rejected there — the white wine + no tomato + ginger/turmeric combination suits the french-onion register much better than it suited the beef stew register.

DIVERGENCES FROM VARIANT A:
- BROADER VEGETABLES: alongside the deeply-caramelized onions, add GARLIC, coarse-chopped CELERY ROOT, TURNIPS, CARROTS, and coarse-chopped or grated GINGER ROOT (a real structural ingredient here, not just a spice). WHITE BEANS folded in for protein (same as variant A). NO POTATOES — see note on why potatoes don't work here.
- HERB / SPICE AXIS: skip the thyme. Use FRESH GINGER + TURMERIC as the main herb/spice axis (plus bay leaf as the quiet anchor).
- STOCK: vegetable stock is the default here (variant A can use either; B leans vegetable to keep the register clean).
- NO TOMATO: no tomato paste, no fresh tomato — the white wine + root-vegetable base doesn't want it.
- GRATIN FINISH: same as variant A — toasted bread + generous gruyere broiled on top.

INGREDIENTS:
- 3-4 large yellow onions, thinly sliced (deep-caramelize as in variant A)
- 3-4 cloves garlic, minced
- 4 tbsp butter
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 bay leaf
- 1-2 inches fresh GINGER ROOT (larger quantity than 'a spice' — coarse-chopped or grated, part of the vegetable base)
- 1/2 to 1 tsp turmeric
- 1/2 to 3/4 cup dry white wine (deglaze)
- 6-8 cups vegetable stock
- 1 medium CELERY ROOT, peeled and coarse-chopped
- 2-3 TURNIPS, peeled and coarse-chopped
- 2-3 CARROTS, coarse-chopped
- 1 can WHITE BEANS (cannellini or great northern), drained and rinsed
- 1 baguette, sliced into rounds and toasted
- shredded gruyere cheese (generous)
- fresh parsley (finish)
- salt and black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. DEEPLY CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: same as variant A — 45-60 min medium-low, mahogany color, real fond.
2. ADD GARLIC briefly (~1 min) before deglazing.
3. DEGLAZE WITH WHITE WINE: as variant A.
4. ADD BROTH + VEGETABLES + HERBS/SPICES: pour in vegetable stock. Add celery root, turnips, carrots, chopped ginger root, turmeric, and bay leaf. Bring to a simmer.
5. SIMMER UNTIL VEGETABLES ARE TENDER: 25-35 min depending on how coarse the chop is.
6. FOLD IN WHITE BEANS: add and simmer 10-15 min to integrate.
7. TASTE AND ADJUST: salt and pepper. Fish out bay leaf.
8. TOAST THE BREAD: as variant A.
9. GRATIN + SERVE: as variant A — bowls, toast, gruyere, broil. Fresh parsley on top.
notes:
=== DEEP CARAMELIZATION IS THE WHOLE TECHNIQUE ===

The onions need to go past standard softened-golden into deep-mahogany-brown territory. This is 45-60 minutes on medium-low, stirred occasionally, not high-heat-quick-sauté. The Maillard reaction across that long slow cook is what generates the sweet-savory-deep flavor that carries the whole soup. Under-caramelize and the soup reads thin and one-note-oniony. Standard shortcuts (adding baking soda to speed browning, high heat with constant stirring) don't produce the same depth.

You'll know it's right when the onions are visibly darker than golden — brown enough that you might worry you overcooked them — and the pot bottom has a substantial fond built up. That fond is what gets deglazed by the wine and dissolves into the finished broth.

=== BEEF STOCK IS THE CLASSICAL CHOICE — BUT DARK VEGETABLE BOUILLON WORKS BETTER (BETTER THAN BOUILLON) ===

Beef stock is the traditional pick for french onion soup, but in practice I find DARK VEGETABLE BOUILLON (specifically Better Than Bouillon's dark vegetable base) works BETTER than beef base here. This holds across both variants — the deeply-caramelized onions carry the savory-hearty register on their own, and the dark vegetable bouillon extends that same register more cleanly than beef base does. Reach for it as the default; keep beef stock as the fallback if that's what you have.

Standard vegetable stock (not the dark/concentrated bouillon paste) still works fine — just not as well as the dark vegetable bouillon.

=== WHITE BEANS FOLDED IN FOR PROTEIN (PERSONALIZATION) ===

A can of cannellini or great northern beans folded in during the simmer gives the soup a protein component that classical french onion soup lacks. The soup is traditionally about the onion + broth + cheese contrast, with no protein — this addition shifts the dish toward a fuller meal rather than a starter or side. If you don't want the protein element (variant A only — variant B is built around the beans), skip them and the recipe still works.

The beans also add a soft creamy textural contrast against the mostly-liquid broth and the toothy caramelized onions. Simmer them in for 15-20 min so they warm through and pick up some of the broth flavor, but not so long that they break down entirely.

GOOD OPPORTUNITY FOR 'LARGE' WHITE BEANS (CORONA / GIGANTES): this soup is a good place to reach for large white beans — CORONA BEANS (also called gigantes) if you can find them. The generous broth + gratin format gives large beans room to be a distinct component on the spoon rather than getting lost the way they might in a tighter dish. Anything works though — regular cannellini or great northern are still totally fine.

=== GRUYERE IS THE CLASSICAL CHEESE — DON'T SUBSTITUTE ===

Gruyere's nutty-sharp alpine character melts cleanly and browns well under the broiler; it's the pick for this soup. Comté would be a close alternative if you have it; regular melting cheeses (mozzarella, monterrey jack) would melt but wouldn't carry the same flavor depth. Sharp cheddar would push the soup toward an anglo register that fights the french identity. Stick with gruyere.

Use plenty — the gratin cheese layer should be substantial, not stingy. Cheese covers the toast and drapes over the bowl's rim; that's the target visual.

=== TOAST THE BREAD FIRST — CRUCIAL FOR STRUCTURE ===

Untoasted bread on top of the soup goes soggy under the broiler and dissolves into the broth as you eat. Pre-toasted rounds hold their crisp structure even after floating in hot broth under melted cheese — you get a distinct crouton-in-cheese-in-broth texture instead of bread pudding. Toast the rounds until they're crisp all the way through, not just surface-browned.

=== OVEN-SAFE BOWLS FOR THE BROILER STEP ===

Traditional presentation uses individual oven-safe crocks or bowls that go directly under the broiler with the cheese on top. If you don't have oven-safe bowls, you can broil the cheese on the toast separately on a sheet pan and then float the finished cheese-toasts on top of the soup at serving — different presentation, same flavor.

=== TURMERIC IS THE SECRET INGREDIENT (VARIANT A) — MAKES IT SMOKEY ===

A pinch of turmeric added to variant A is the secret ingredient — it makes the finished soup taste smokey. Not a classical french onion soup ingredient; keeps the origin of the smoky note hidden. Don't tell anyone.

In variant B turmeric is upgraded to a real herb/spice-axis ingredient (1/2 to 1 tsp) alongside fresh ginger root, not just a secret pinch.

=== NO POTATOES IN VARIANT B — THEY'RE FOR PAIRING WITH (PSEUDO)MEAT, NOT OTHER VEGETABLES ===

Potatoes were originally in variant B; removed. They don't work here. The reasoning: potatoes are designed to pair with (pseudo)meat in a broth-based dish, not with other vegetables. In a pure-vegetable soup like variant B, potatoes fight the celery-root + turnip + carrot register rather than extending it. Skip potatoes here; if you want a starch in the soup, the toasted bread + gruyere gratin is doing that job.

Where potatoes DO belong: variant B of french-beef-and-mushroom-stew (with pseudo-meat), where they're explicitly load-bearing.

=== WANT TO TRY — PARSNIPS IN VARIANT B ===

Parsnips are a candidate for variant B alongside the celery root + turnips + carrots register. They'd fit the sweet-root-vegetable slot the current variant is built around. Untested; log when tried.

=== VARIANT B FRAMING — WHY WHITE WINE + NO TOMATO + GINGER/TURMERIC SUITS THIS DISH (BUT NOT FRENCH BEEF STEW) ===

An earlier attempt drafted these ideas as a pure-vegetable variant of french-beef-and-mushroom-stew (celery root/turnips instead of meat, ginger + turmeric instead of rosemary + thyme, no tomato, white wine). That variant was rejected — it didn't work well in the beef-stew register.

The reason it works here as variant B: the classical french onion soup framework is already built around white wine, no tomato, and deeply-caramelized onions carrying the flavor. Extending outward from that base into celery root + potatoes + carrots + ginger root keeps the register consistent. In the beef-stew register (red wine + tomato + rosemary + meat/pseudo-meat), the same ingredient set fought the base rather than extended from it.

If you want a pure-vegetable french stew-adjacent dish, variant B here is the right home — not a variant of the beef stew.

=== PARSLEY AT THE FINISH ===

Chopped fresh parsley scattered on top of the finished bowl before serving.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- french-chicken-soup: french soup with chicken thighs + white wine + herbs + dumplings. Broth-forward format, different protein logic (chicken meat), same french-provincial axis.
- lentil-mushroom-potato-stew: french/italian vegetable stew. Also uses beef or vegetable stock; different structural logic (chunky stew vs onion-and-broth soup).
- coq-au-vin: french chicken braise with red wine and mushrooms. Different food, similar occasion.
